name: Ahimaaz
title: Son of Zadok and messenger for King David
summary:
Ahimaaz, son of the high priest Zadok, played a crucial role during Absalom's rebellion against King David.  
Together with Jonathan, son of Abiathar, he formed a central part of David's intelligence network.  
The two were stationed at En-Rogel outside Jerusalem to receive strategic information from Hushai, David's advisor who operated as a double agent in Absalom's court.  
After a dramatic escape where they were hidden in a well in Bahurim, they reached David with the life-saving message to cross the Jordan without delay.  
Ahimaaz also distinguished himself after the victory over Absalom's army by insisting on running to David with news of the triumph, despite Joab's objections.  
He showed both physical endurance and diplomatic wisdom — he told David about the victory but refrained from revealing Absalom's death.  
In the priestly lineage, he is regarded as the father of Azariah, and thus belongs to the Zadokite priestly line that played a prominent role in temple service in Jerusalem.  
It is also possible that he is identical with the Ahimaaz mentioned as one of Solomon's district governors over the territory of Naphtali.

keyEvents.title: Stationed as a spy at En-Rogel
keyEvents.description: Ahimaaz and Jonathan, son of Abiathar, were stationed at En-Rogel outside Jerusalem to receive intelligence from Hushai and pass it on to David, who had fled the city during Absalom's rebellion.

keyEvents.title: Hidden in a well in Bahurim
keyEvents.description: When Absalom's servants searched for Ahimaaz and Jonathan, they were hidden in a well by a woman in Bahurim, who covered the well with a cloth and scattered grain over it so that the pursuers did not find them.

keyEvents.title: Brought news to David about Ahithophel's advice
keyEvents.description: After escaping their pursuers, Ahimaaz and Jonathan brought the vital message to David that he must cross the Jordan immediately, since Ahithophel had advised Absalom to pursue him at once.

keyEvents.title: Running from the battlefield
keyEvents.description: After the victory over Absalom's forces, Ahimaaz insisted on running to David with the news, despite Joab's attempt to stop him. He ran via the Jordan Valley and arrived before the Cushite whom Joab had sent.

keyEvents.title: Delivering the news of victory to David
keyEvents.description: When Ahimaaz reached David, he reported the victory but tactfully omitted telling about Absalom's death. The watchman had already recognized him by his running style. It was the Cushite who then brought the painful news of Absalom's fall.

keyEvents.title: Possible identification as Solomon's district governor
keyEvents.description: An Ahimaaz is mentioned as one of King Solomon's twelve district governors, married to Solomon's daughter Basemath and responsible for the Naphtali region. It is debated whether this is the same Ahimaaz as Zadok's son.

versions.summary: Ahimaaz was the son of the high priest Zadok and served as a loyal messenger for King David during Absalom's rebellion. He is best known for running from the battlefield to bring David news of victory over Absalom. His loyalty and courage made him an important figure in David's circle during one of the most dramatic periods in Israel's history.
versions.title: Zadok's son and messenger
versions.reason: [major] Ahimaaz is not described as a 'warrior' in the biblical text. He was primarily a messenger/ambassador and a priest's son. The role 'warrior' should be replaced with 'messenger'.; [minor] 2 Sam 15:27 and 15:36 should be listed as separate verses in the array, not just [27, 36], since this could be misinterpreted as referring only to verse 27 and 36. However, it is technically correct as individual verse numbers. Nevertheless, one should consider including verse 35, which also mentions Zadok and Abiathar and their sons.; [minor] There is biblical uncertainty about whether the Ahimaaz mentioned in 1 Kgs 4:15 is the same Ahimaaz who was Zadok's son. The description should reflect this uncertainty more clearly.; [minor] That Azariah was the son of Ahimaaz is mentioned in 1 Chr 6:8-9, but this could potentially refer to another Azariah in the priestly lineage. Nevertheless, it remains the most accepted interpretation, so it can stand.; [minor] The summary is good, but should mention that Ahimaaz was a priest's son and that his role as a messenger was connected to the spy network David organized during his flight from Absalom.; [major] Footnotes are missing that could shed light on the historical, linguistic, and theological aspects of Ahimaaz's role.

versions.summary: Ahimaaz was the son of the high priest Zadok and served as a loyal messenger and spy for King David during Absalom's rebellion. Together with Jonathan, the son of Abiathar, he formed an important part of David's intelligence network in Jerusalem. The two were stationed at En-Rogel outside the city to receive information from Hushai, David's advisor who operated as a double agent at Absalom's court. Ahimaaz is especially known for insisting on running from the battlefield to bring David news of the victory over Absalom's forces, where he tactfully omitted telling him about Absalom's death. His loyalty, courage, and swift feet made him a key figure during one of the most dramatic periods of David's reign.

versions.summary:
Ahimaaz, son of the high priest Zadok, played a crucial role during Absalom's rebellion against King David.  
As part of a well-developed intelligence network, he was stationed with Jonathan, son of Abiathar, at En-Rogel outside Jerusalem to receive strategic information from Hushai — David's advisor who operated as a double agent in Absalom's court.  
After a dramatic escape where they were hidden in a cistern in Bahurim, they brought David the life-saving message to cross the Jordan.  
Ahimaaz is especially known for his run from the battlefield after the victory over Absalom's army, where he insisted on bringing the news to David despite Joab's objections.  
He showed both courage and diplomatic wisdom by reporting the victory but refraining from revealing Absalom's death.  
In the priestly lineage, he is regarded as the father of Azariah and thus belongs to the Zadokite priestly line that became highly significant for temple service in Jerusalem.

footnotes.text: The name Ahimaaz (Hebrew: אֲחִימַעַץ, Achimaʿats) probably means 'my brother is wrath' or 'brother of the counselor'. The name appears in several places in the Old Testament and may refer to different individuals, including Saul's father-in-law (1 Sam 14:50).

En-Rogel, where Ahimaaz and Jonathan were stationed as spies, was a spring just south of Jerusalem at the confluence of the Hinnom Valley and the Kidron Valley. The site was strategically located outside the city walls so that messengers could receive information without entering the city. The spring is traditionally identified with Bi'r Ayyub (Job's Well) in present-day Jerusalem.

Bahurim, where Ahimaaz and Jonathan were hidden in a well, was a village on the east side of the Mount of Olives near the road down to the Jordan Valley. The place is also known from the episode where Shimei cursed David (2 Sam 16:5). The exact location is uncertain, but it is often associated with Ras et-Tmim east of the Mount of Scopus.

The fact that Ahimaaz ran via 'the plain' (Hebrew: כִּכָּר, kikkar) — the Jordan Plain — and yet arrived before the Cushite suggests he was an exceptionally fast runner. The watchman recognized him by his running style from a distance (2 Sam 18:27), indicating that he was known for his athletic ability.

In the priestly genealogy in 1 Chr 5:34-36 (in some numbering systems 6:8-10), Ahimaaz is mentioned as the son of Zadok and father of Azariah. This Azariah may be the high priest who served in Solomon's temple (cf. 2 Chr 6:10), which would place Ahimaaz in a central position within the Zadokite priesthood that dominated temple service in Jerusalem.

Joab's reluctance to let Ahimaaz bring news of Absalom's death can be interpreted as an attempt to protect the priest's son from David's potential anger. In the ancient Near East, it was a known risk to bring bad news to kings, and Joab instead sent a Cushite — possibly a slave or soldier of lower status.

Ahimaaz's role as an intelligence agent reflects a sophisticated military organization in David's kingdom. The use of a network with Hushai as a double agent, priestly sons as couriers, and a woman in Bahurim as a co-conspirator testifies to a well-thought-out intelligence structure.

The Hebrew verb for Ahimaaz's running (רוץ, ruts) is used repeatedly in 2 Sam 18, and the text emphasizes that the watchman recognized his characteristic running style (מְרוּצַת, merutsat). This may indicate that Ahimaaz was a professional runner or courier, a role with military and administrative significance in ancient Israel.
